parole.significato: a black grape variety from Basilicata and Campania
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan aglianeca, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: to turn on, to arouse sexually
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan arrapà, of unclear origin (see there for hypotheses)

parole.significato: a light turnover of dough filled with mozzarella (or similar cheese), anchovies and parsley
parole.testo: From calzone + -cello (diminutive suffix), calque of Neapolitan cazunciello.
From a Neapolitan word supposedly from Spanish camorra (“dispute, quarrel”).
Borrowed from Neapolitan cazziare. Doublet of cazzeggiare.

parole.significato: opportunistic and cynical use of stratagems
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan cazzimma, from cazzo (“dick”) + -imma.
Borrowed from Neapolitan, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us, from *pleth₂- (“flat”). Doublet of piatto (“flat”).
Originally a Neapolitan cognate of cetriolo.
Borrowed from Neapolitan ciuccio. Ultimately a variant of ciuco (“donkey”).

Possibly, through Neapolitan, from Latin phalanga (“pole for carrying things”, by extension “pole for sustaining grapevine”), from Ancient Greek φᾰ́λᾰγξ (phắlănx, “line, rank”), Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, plank”). Compare falanga and falange.
Borrowed from Neapolitan femmeniello (“little woman”), from femmena (“woman”) + iello (masculine diminutive).
Borrowed from Neapolitan. By surface analysis, figlio (“son”) + -anda.

parole.significato: fumarole (opening in the ground that emits gases)
parole.testo: From Neapolitan fumarola, from Late Latin fūmāriolum, diminutive of fūmārium (“chimney”), from Latin fumus (“smoke”), 16th c. Compare Sicilian fumalora.
Borrowed from Neapolitan guaglione.

parole.significato: jinx (person supposed to bring bad luck)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan jettatore. Doublet of gettatore.
From Neapolitan 'nciucio (“gossip”).
Borrowed from Neapolitan mannaggia (“damn!”, literally “may he/she/it have bad things from it!”). Compare with Sicilian mannaja.

Ultimate origin unknown. The Italian word was borrowed from Neapolitan mariuolo and gradually spread throughout Italy, with the Neapolitan word possibly originating from the French mariole. Compare the standard Italian mariolo.
From Neapolitan.

Borrowed from Neapolitan, the equivalent of Italian immondizia and immondezza, from Latin immunditia (“dirt, untidiness”), from immundus (“dirty”), from im- (“without, not”) + mundus (“clean, elegant”). Doublet of immondizia and immondezza. Compare Sicilian munnizza.

parole.significato: a smooth, tube-shaped form of pasta, similar to very large macaroni
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan.

parole.significato: a form of street-food sandwich from Campania, served hot
parole.testo: From Neapolitan panuozzo, from pane (“bread”) + -uozzo (alteration-forming suffix). Equivalent to pane + -ozzo.
From Neapolitan pernacchio, from earlier vernacchio, from Latin vernāculus (“of or pertaining to a slave”). Doublet of vernacolo.
From the present participle of pezzire, from (Old) Neapolitan pezzire, from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere.

parole.significato: a pigeon; more accurately the rock pigeon, feral pigeon or domestic pigeon
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem. Doublet of pippione.

First attested in 1590, as Neapolitan pizza (Velardiniello, La storia de cient'anne arreto). Likely related to Byzantine Greek πίτα (píta, “cake, pie”) (12th century); the origin of the Greek word is itself uncertain. Also possibly from Lombardic bizza (also pizza or bizzo (pizzo), which would rathe
Borrowed from Neapolitan pummarola (“tomato”), in turn an alteration of Italian pomodoro (literally “golden fruit, golden apple”).

parole.significato: escabeche (a dish of fried fish, or other food, marinated in vinegar)
parole.testo: Neapolitan derivative of Spanish escabeche, from Arabic اَلسِّكْبَاجَة (as-sikbāja). Cf. ceviche.
From Neapolitan scarrupo, sgarrupo, of uncertain origin.
Borrowed from Neapolitan scetavajasse (literally “maid-waker”), from sceta (“wake up”, imperative of scetà) + vajasse (“maids, female servants”, plural of vajassa).

parole.significato: to snatch (especially to steal a bag)
parole.testo: Unknown, of Neapolitan origin.

parole.significato: luxury, pomp, grandeur, sumptuousness, magnificence, éclat
parole.testo: From Neapolitan sfarzo, sfarzare, from Spanish disfrazar (“to disguise”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: a traditional Christmas sweet from Naples in the form of little balls of fried dough, sweetened and flavoured/flavored…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan struffule, of uncertain origin: possibly from Ancient Greek στρογγύλος (strongúlos, “round, spherical”).

parole.significato: droveway, sheep track, commonly found in Southern Italy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan, from Latin tractōrius (“of or relating to drawing and hoisting”), from trahō, trahere (“to draw, hoist”), whence Italian trarre.
Borrowed from Neapolitan vongola, from Latin conchula, from concha. Displaced Old Italian gongola.

parole.significato: a street peddler, especially one of non-European origin
parole.testo: An altering of vuoi comprare? (“do you want to buy?”), meant to sound non-native. More likely borrowed from a Southern Italian language, such as Neapolitan vu' cumprà? (“do you want to buy?”). Because of the racist undertone of imitating a stereotypical foreign accent, the word is considered unfit f
Borrowed from Neapolitan zompare.
From cacio (“cheese”) + cavallo (“horse”), inherited from Old Italian. More likely calqued from Neapolitan, or Sicilian casucavaḍḍu (or from dialectal cascavaḍḍu). Doublet of cosacavaddu.
